lessons.title: Measuring the Global Burden of Disease
body: Global health begins with a counting problem: how do you compare a death from malaria in a toddler with years of disabling depression in an adult? The standard answer is the disability-adjusted life year, or DALY. One DALY is one healthy year of life lost. It is the sum of years of life lost to premature death (YLL) and years lived with disability (YLD), where each year with a condition is weighted between 0 (full health) and 1 (equivalent to death) by a disability weight. A death at age 5 costs many years of life lost; a chronic, non-fatal condition such as low back pain or major depression costs few YLL but a great deal of YLD.

The Global Burden of Disease study, run by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation and collaborators, estimates deaths, DALYs and risk-factor attributions for hundreds of conditions across countries and years. The World Health Organization publishes its own Global Health Estimates using a related but not identical methodology, so figures for the same year can differ. Learners should treat any single number as a modelled estimate with uncertainty, especially for countries with weak death registration, where deaths must be inferred from surveys and verbal autopsies.

Two patterns dominate the picture. First, over the past few decades life expectancy has risen in nearly every region and under-five mortality has fallen sharply, from roughly 12 million deaths a year around 1990 to under 5 million in recent estimates (approximate figures). Second, the leading causes of death have shifted. Noncommunicable diseases (ischaemic heart disease, stroke, cancers, chronic respiratory disease, diabetes) now account for roughly three quarters of deaths worldwide by WHO estimates. In low-income countries, however, infectious diseases, neonatal conditions, maternal conditions and malnutrition still make up a much larger share, so many low-income countries carry a double burden: the old problems have not gone away while the new ones arrive.

A ranking by deaths and a ranking by DALYs can differ. Depressive disorders, hearing loss and musculoskeletal conditions rank high in DALYs because they cause disability over many years, even though they cause few deaths directly. Neonatal conditions rank high in both because each death costs a whole lifetime. This is why policy debates about priorities depend on which metric is chosen, and why DALYs are used in cost-effectiveness analysis, usually expressed as cost per DALY averted.

Critics note that DALYs embed value judgements: disability weights are derived from surveys of the public and health professionals, early versions weighted years of life by age, and a single number can hide who bears the burden. Defenders reply that an explicit, transparent metric is better than implicit judgement, and that modern versions have dropped age weighting and discounting in the headline figures.

Worked example: a disease kills 1,000 people at an age where each would have had 20 more years, giving 20,000 YLL. A second condition leaves 10,000 people with a disability of weight 0.2 for one year, giving 2,000 YLD in that year. The first burden is larger in this snapshot, but if the second condition lasts ten years in each person the cumulative YLD reaches 20,000, which is why duration matters.

lessons.title: Social Determinants of Health
body: The social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live and age, and the wider systems that shape those conditions: income, education, employment, housing, neighbourhood, discrimination, and access to services. The central claim is that these factors explain much of the variation in health between and within countries, often more than medical care does. Medical care repairs damage; social conditions largely decide who is exposed to the damage in the first place.

The classic evidence is the social gradient. In the Whitehall studies of British civil servants, led by Michael Marmot, mortality rose steadily as employment grade fell, even though everyone had stable jobs and access to a national health service. The gradient was not limited to the poorest group; each step down the hierarchy carried worse health. This suggests that relative position, control over one's work and exposure to stress matter in addition to material deprivation. Cross-country comparisons point the same way: life expectancy is not simply tied to national income, and some middle-income countries outperform richer ones because of broad education, primary care and social protection.

The WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health reported in 2008 under the title Closing the Gap in a Generation. Its three overarching recommendations were to improve daily living conditions, to tackle the inequitable distribution of power, money and resources, and to measure and understand the problem and assess the impact of action. The Dahlgren-Whitehead model is a common teaching diagram: individual lifestyle sits at the centre, wrapped in social and community networks, then living and working conditions, then general socioeconomic, cultural and environmental conditions.

A useful distinction is between downstream, midstream and upstream action. Downstream means treating illness (a clinic that prescribes insulin). Midstream addresses behaviours and exposures (a smoking cessation programme). Upstream changes the conditions that drive exposure (tobacco taxation, school meals, safe housing, minimum wage law). Upstream measures often have the largest population effect but are slow, political and hard to attribute. The Ottawa Charter of 1986 and the later Health in All Policies approach argue that sectors outside health, such as transport, education and finance, should assess the health impact of their decisions.

There are cautions. Association is not always causation: sick people may fall in income (reverse causation), and unmeasured factors can confound. Researchers address this with natural experiments and longitudinal designs, such as studies of conditional cash transfer programmes, which in several Latin American settings improved school attendance and some health outcomes. Another caution is that framing everything as a social determinant should not become an excuse for neglecting effective clinical services.

Worked example: two neighbouring districts have the same number of clinics but a twelve-year difference in life expectancy. Investigators find differences in housing quality, air pollution, job security and food access. The determinants framing predicts that adding clinics alone will narrow the gap only modestly, while action on housing and income would narrow it more.

lessons.title: Transitions, Equity and Inequality Measurement
body: Populations change in predictable ways as societies develop, and global health planning depends on knowing where a country sits on the path. The demographic transition describes a shift from high birth and death rates to low ones. Death rates fall first (better nutrition, sanitation, vaccines), producing rapid population growth; birth rates then fall (education, particularly of girls, contraception, urbanisation, lower child mortality), and growth slows and the population ages. The epidemiologic transition, described by Abdel Omran in 1971, is the matching shift in disease: from pandemics of infection and famine, to receding pandemics, to an age of degenerative and man-made diseases such as heart disease and cancer.

Countries move at different speeds and not in a single line. Many low- and middle-income countries are experiencing a polarised or protracted transition, with urban elites developing noncommunicable disease patterns while rural poor populations still face infection and undernutrition, and with the same household sometimes containing both stunted children and an overweight adult. This double burden of malnutrition, and the broader double burden of communicable plus noncommunicable disease, means that a health system built for acute infection must also learn chronic care.

Equity needs to be separated from equality. Equality means giving everyone the same. Health equity means that avoidable and unfair differences in health are reduced, which may require giving more to those with greater need. The word inequity is used for differences that are both avoidable and unjust; a difference in prostate cancer rates between men and women is a difference but not an inequity.

Inequality is measured with several tools. The simplest is a gap or ratio between two groups, such as under-five mortality in the richest versus poorest wealth quintile. The slope index of inequality and the relative index of inequality use all groups ranked by socioeconomic position. The concentration index, derived from the concentration curve, ranges from -1 to +1; a negative value means the health variable (such as ill-health) is concentrated among the poor. Data often come from household surveys such as the Demographic and Health Surveys, which also let analysts disaggregate by sex, residence, ethnicity and education.

Averages can hide inequality: a national under-five mortality rate can improve while the rate among the poorest quintile stagnates. This is the logic behind the Sustainable Development Goals' pledge to leave no one behind, and behind the idea of progressive universalism, in which a system expands coverage for all but sequences the expansion so that the worst-off gain first.

Worked example: a country's poorest quintile has under-five mortality falling from 140 to 100 per 1,000 while the richest falls from 60 to 20. The absolute gap is 80 before (140 minus 60) and 80 after (100 minus 20), so it is unchanged, while the ratio grew from about 2.3 to 5. Absolute and relative measures can tell different stories, so both should be reported.

lessons.title: Maternal, Newborn and Child Health
body: Maternal and child mortality are treated as sentinel indicators because they reflect the strength of an entire health system. The maternal mortality ratio is the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. A maternal death is the death of a woman during pregnancy or within 42 days of its end from causes related to or aggravated by the pregnancy, excluding accidental causes. Sustainable Development Goal 3 sets a target of fewer than 70 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030, and for children an under-five mortality of at most 25 per 1,000 live births and neonatal mortality of at most 12 per 1,000.

The leading direct causes of maternal death are obstetric haemorrhage, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (pre-eclampsia and eclampsia), sepsis, complications of unsafe abortion and obstructed labour; indirect causes include malaria, HIV and anaemia worsened by pregnancy. Most of these deaths occur around delivery and in the first day postpartum, and nearly all are preventable. The Three Delays model of Thaddeus and Maine explains why women die even when care exists: delay in deciding to seek care, delay in reaching a facility, and delay in receiving adequate care once there.

Effective interventions follow from the causes. Skilled attendance at birth and access to emergency obstetric care address obstructed labour and haemorrhage. Uterotonics, especially oxytocin given after delivery, and tranexamic acid reduce death from bleeding. Magnesium sulfate prevents seizures in severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. Antenatal care, tetanus vaccination, iron and folate supplementation, and family planning reduce risk before and between pregnancies; contraception averts deaths by averting high-risk pregnancies.

For children, the big killers outside the neonatal period are pneumonia, diarrhoeal disease, malaria and malnutrition, with a large share of under-five deaths occurring in the first 28 days of life from prematurity, birth asphyxia and neonatal infection. Low-cost, high-impact tools include oral rehydration salts with zinc for diarrhoea, antibiotics for pneumonia, immunisation, insecticide-treated nets and malaria treatment, exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, and kangaroo mother care (prolonged skin-to-skin contact) for small babies. The WHO and UNICEF package called Integrated Management of Childhood Illness trains first-level health workers to assess a sick child for several conditions at once rather than treating a single complaint, so that a child with cough, fever and poor feeding is not sent home after one problem is addressed.

Community health workers are central: they can distribute oral rehydration, test and treat malaria with rapid tests, and counsel on breastfeeding and danger signs. Trials and programme evaluations of community case management have shown reductions in child mortality, though results depend on supervision, supply of medicines and referral.

Worked example: a rural woman bleeds after a home birth. Her family debates whether to go (delay one), the nearest facility is four hours by foot over a flooded road (delay two), and on arrival the clinic has no oxytocin or blood (delay three). Training a birth attendant alone would not have saved her; the solution is a package across all three delays: community awareness, transport and facility readiness.

lessons.title: Vaccination Programmes and Eradication
body: Vaccination is the most cost-effective tool in public health because protection extends beyond the individual. Herd immunity occurs when enough of a population is immune that an infection cannot sustain transmission. For a simple model, the threshold proportion immune is 1 minus 1 divided by R0, where R0 is the basic reproduction number, the average number of people one case infects in a fully susceptible population. Measles has an R0 commonly cited between about 12 and 18, so around 95 percent coverage with two doses is needed to prevent outbreaks. For an infection with R0 of 4, the threshold is 75 percent, and because no vaccine is perfect, coverage must exceed that: with a vaccine that is 90 percent effective the required coverage is about 0.75 divided by 0.9, or 83 percent.

Programmes organise delivery. The World Health Assembly launched the Expanded Programme on Immunization in 1974 to bring a core set of childhood vaccines to all children. Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, created in 2000, pools donor funds and purchasing power so lower-income countries can introduce newer vaccines such as pneumococcal conjugate, rotavirus and HPV, usually with co-financing that rises as a country's income grows. Coverage is tracked by indicators such as the share of infants receiving a third dose of DTP-containing vaccine. Zero-dose children, who have received no routine vaccines, are concentrated in conflict zones, remote areas and urban slums, and are a priority group. The cold chain, a system of refrigerated storage and transport from manufacturer to health post, is a practical constraint: many vaccines degrade if heated or, for some, frozen.

Smallpox is the model success. Intensified campaigns using surveillance and ring vaccination, which vaccinates the contacts of cases and their contacts rather than whole populations, stopped transmission; the last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977 and the World Health Assembly declared eradication in 1980. Smallpox was suited to eradication because it had no animal reservoir, visible disease, lasting immunity and an effective vaccine. Polio eradication has been harder. The Global Polio Eradication Initiative began in 1988; wild poliovirus types 2 and 3 have been certified eradicated, while type 1 remains endemic in Afghanistan and Pakistan as of this writing.

Polio also shows a trade-off in vaccine design. The oral polio vaccine uses live attenuated virus, is cheap, easy to give and induces gut immunity, but in rare cases in under-immunised communities the vaccine virus can circulate, mutate and regain neurovirulence, causing circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus. The inactivated vaccine, given by injection, cannot do this but is costlier and induces less intestinal immunity. The programme therefore combines both and is moving to newer oral formulations designed to be more genetically stable.

Vaccine acceptance is a policy issue as well as a technical one. WHO advisers describe confidence, complacency and convenience as factors that shape uptake. Strategies that work include trusted messengers, reducing wait times and cost, reminder systems and, in some places, school-entry requirements; the evidence on mandates is mixed and the ethics are debated, with some arguing that they protect vulnerable people and others that they risk eroding trust.

Worked example: a district has 82 percent measles coverage with first doses and recurring outbreaks. Reasoning from herd thresholds, coverage is well below roughly 95 percent, and pockets of unvaccinated children cluster geographically. The remedy is a catch-up campaign plus a second routine dose and outreach to the zero-dose pockets, not a change in vaccine type.

lessons.title: Malaria: Biology and Control
body: Malaria is caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium, transmitted by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Five species infect humans: Plasmodium falciparum (the most lethal, and dominant in sub-Saharan Africa), P. vivax (widespread outside Africa), P. ovale, P. malariae and the zoonotic P. knowlesi. Sporozoites injected by the mosquito travel to the liver, multiply, and release merozoites that invade red blood cells, where cycles of replication and rupture cause fever, anaemia and, in falciparum, sequestration of infected cells in small vessels that produces cerebral malaria and organ failure. P. vivax and P. ovale can form dormant liver stages called hypnozoites, which cause relapse weeks or months later.

The burden falls heavily on sub-Saharan Africa, which carries the great majority of cases and deaths, and on young children and pregnant women. Children lose maternal antibody protection and have not yet acquired partial immunity, which develops only after repeated infection and wanes without exposure. Some genetic traits modify risk: sickle cell trait protects against severe falciparum malaria, and Duffy-negative red cells resist P. vivax, which uses the Duffy antigen to enter.

Control uses layered tools. Vector control relies on insecticide-treated bed nets, which kill or deter mosquitoes that bite at night, and indoor residual spraying of walls; resistance of mosquitoes to pyrethroids has driven development of nets that add a second active ingredient. Prevention in groups at high risk includes seasonal malaria chemoprevention, in which children in areas with strongly seasonal transmission, such as the Sahel, receive courses of antimalarials through the rainy season, and intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy using sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine. Diagnosis in the field uses rapid diagnostic tests that detect parasite antigens, with microscopy as the reference method; treating on suspicion alone wastes drugs and misses other causes of fever.

Treatment of uncomplicated falciparum malaria uses artemisinin-based combination therapy, which pairs a fast-acting artemisinin derivative with a longer-acting partner drug, reducing resistance risk. Severe malaria is treated with intravenous artesunate. The discovery of artemisinin by Tu Youyou, drawing on classical Chinese medical texts, earned a Nobel Prize in 2015. For P. vivax and P. ovale, a drug active against hypnozoites, such as primaquine or tafenoquine, is needed to prevent relapse; because these can cause haemolysis in people with G6PD deficiency, testing or careful risk assessment is required.

Threats and advances: partial resistance to artemisinin, first found in Southeast Asia, has been confirmed in parts of East Africa, and monitoring and drug-combination strategies are priorities. Two vaccines for children, RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M, have been recommended by WHO; both give partial protection and are added to, not replacing, other tools.

Worked example: a child in the Sahel presents in the rainy season with fever and a positive rapid test. Treatment is an artemisinin-based combination. The public-health response in the district includes net coverage, seasonal chemoprevention for eligible children and surveillance for drug resistance.

lessons.title: Tuberculosis Control
body: Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and spreads through the air when a person with active pulmonary disease coughs. Most people who are infected contain the bacteria in a latent state and never become ill; a minority progress to active disease, the risk being highest in the first years after infection and in people with HIV, malnutrition, diabetes, tobacco or silica exposure, or immunosuppressive treatment. Before COVID-19, tuberculosis was the world's leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, and it has regained that position in WHO reporting as of this writing. Most cases occur in a group of high-burden countries in Asia and Africa.

The core diagnostic and treatment challenge is that the organism grows slowly and is hard to kill. Standard drug-susceptible disease is treated for six months: two months of isoniazid, rifampicin (rifampin), pyrazinamide and ethambutol, followed by four months of isoniazid and rifampicin. Each drug has well-known adverse effects. Isoniazid can cause hepatitis and peripheral neuropathy, the latter reduced by giving pyridoxine (vitamin B6). Rifampicin is a strong inducer of liver enzymes and so interacts with many drugs, including some antiretrovirals and hormonal contraceptives, and turns body fluids orange. Pyrazinamide raises uric acid and can cause hepatitis. Ethambutol can cause optic neuritis, so visual acuity and colour vision matter.

Because treatment is long, adherence is a core problem. The WHO strategy called DOTS (directly observed treatment, short-course) combined political commitment, reliable microscopy, a secure drug supply, standardised regimens and observed therapy with monitoring. Later strategies, namely Stop TB and the End TB Strategy, broadened the approach to include patient support, social protection, and contact tracing. Digital reminders and community support are used alongside observation.

Drug resistance is the great threat. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis is defined as resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin. Resistance arises from incomplete or poorly supervised treatment, poor drug quality, and direct transmission of resistant strains. A major advance was the Xpert MTB/RIF test, a cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test endorsed by WHO in 2010, which detects the bacterium and the rpoB mutation that signals rifampicin resistance within hours. Newer all-oral regimens built on bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, sometimes with moxifloxacin, shortened treatment of resistant disease to about six months and replaced older regimens with injectables that had severe toxicity.

BCG vaccine, given in infancy in many countries, reduces severe childhood forms such as meningitis and miliary disease but gives variable protection against adult pulmonary disease, so new vaccine candidates are under study. Preventive treatment of latent infection in high-risk groups, such as people with HIV and household contacts, is an important complementary strategy.

Worked example: a man with HIV has cough and weight loss and a positive Xpert result that also reports rifampicin resistance. This pattern indicates likely multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, so a rifampicin-based regimen would fail; the clinician moves to a resistant-disease regimen, tests for further resistance and coordinates antiretrovirals because of drug interactions.

lessons.title: HIV: From Epidemic to Control
body: HIV is a retrovirus that infects CD4-positive T cells and, left untreated, depletes them, leading to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and opportunistic infections such as tuberculosis, Pneumocystis pneumonia and cryptococcal meningitis. It spreads through unprotected sex, blood (including shared injecting equipment and unscreened transfusion), and from mother to child during pregnancy, delivery and breastfeeding. Sub-Saharan Africa carries most people living with HIV, with young women and key populations, including men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs and transgender people, at heightened risk in different settings. Stigma, criminalisation and gender inequality are structural drivers that keep people from testing and treatment.

The modern strategy rests on antiretroviral therapy. Combinations of antiretroviral drugs suppress viral replication to levels undetectable in blood. WHO now recommends a first-line regimen based on dolutegravir, an integrase strand transfer inhibitor, combined with two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, typically including tenofovir. Dolutegravir has a high barrier to resistance and generic production has made it affordable in lower-income countries. Suppression has two benefits: the person's health is restored, and transmission is prevented. The HPTN 052 trial found that early treatment of the positive partner in serodiscordant couples sharply reduced sexual transmission, and later studies supported the principle summarised as undetectable equals untransmittable.

Programmatic targets shape policy. UNAIDS set the 95-95-95 targets for 2025: 95 percent of people living with HIV knowing their status, 95 percent of those diagnosed on treatment, and 95 percent of those on treatment with viral suppression. Many countries have approached or reached these in some groups, but gaps remain among men, adolescents and key populations. Funding is volatile and heavily donor-dependent, a point worth tracking: the Global Fund (created in 2002) and the United States President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (launched in 2003) have been major financiers.

Prevention of mother-to-child transmission is one of the great successes. With antiretroviral therapy in pregnancy that suppresses the viral load, safe delivery practices and infant prophylaxis, transmission can fall to a few percent or lower; some countries have been validated as having eliminated mother-to-child transmission. Pre-exposure prophylaxis uses antiretroviral drugs taken by HIV-negative people at risk, originally daily oral tenofovir-based tablets; longer-acting injectable options, including cabotegravir and, as of this writing, the twice-yearly injectable lenacapavir, extend choices and may help people who struggle with daily pills. Post-exposure prophylaxis, given as soon as possible and within 72 hours of exposure, is another tool. Harm reduction for injecting drug use, including needle and syringe programmes and opioid agonist therapy, has strong evidence of reducing transmission.

Worked example: a pregnant woman is diagnosed in the second trimester. She starts dolutegravir-based therapy at once, achieving viral suppression before delivery; her infant gets prophylaxis and testing, and infant feeding is supported with continued maternal treatment. Without treatment her risk of transmission would be high; with it the risk is low.

lessons.title: Outbreak Investigation and Response
body: An outbreak is an occurrence of disease in excess of what is normally expected in a place and time. Responding to one follows a logic that field epidemiologists teach in a standard sequence: confirm that an outbreak exists and verify the diagnosis; define a case, usually with confirmed, probable and suspected categories; find cases actively; describe them by time, place and person; generate hypotheses about source and mode of transmission; test them with an analytic study; put control measures in place without waiting for certainty when risk is high; and communicate findings. The epidemic curve, a histogram of cases by date of onset, hints at the pattern: a sharp single peak suggests a common-source exposure, while successive waves separated by one incubation period suggest person-to-person spread.

Several measures guide response. The incubation period is the time from infection to symptoms; the serial interval is the time between symptom onset in a case and in the person they infect; the case fatality ratio is the proportion of confirmed cases who die. The effective reproduction number, Rt, is the average number of secondary infections at a given time given immunity and control measures; control aims to push it below 1. Surveillance systems, such as the Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response framework promoted in Africa, support early detection through case reporting and laboratory networks, and rumour monitoring can supplement official reports.

The 2014 to 2016 Ebola epidemic in West Africa, centred on Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, illustrates both failure and success. Ebola virus, a filovirus with fruit bats as the likely reservoir, spreads through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of symptomatic people or of the dead; incubation is about 2 to 21 days. Early in the epidemic the signal was missed in a region with weak health systems and porous borders, and the disease reached capital cities. Roughly 28,000 cases and 11,000 deaths were reported (approximate), including large numbers of health workers. The turning point came with a layered response: isolation and treatment units, rigorous infection prevention and control, rapid contact tracing and follow-up for 21 days, safe and dignified burials (funeral practices were a major transmission route), and community engagement that took local leaders and customs seriously rather than treating them as obstacles.

Vaccines and drugs followed. A ring vaccination trial in Guinea in 2015 vaccinated contacts of cases and contacts of contacts with the rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine and gave strong evidence of protection; the vaccine was subsequently licensed. In a later outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a randomised trial of treatments found that two monoclonal antibody products had lower mortality than the comparison therapies, and both were later approved. These products target the Zaire species of Ebola virus, not all filoviruses.

Response is not only technical. Trust is a determinant of success: communities that experienced abrupt quarantines, unexplained burials or distrust of foreign teams sometimes hid cases. Programmes that hired local workers, explained decisions and respected funerals fared better. Another lesson is the cost of delay: the earlier cases are detected and isolated, the smaller the outbreak, which is why investment in surveillance and local capacity is cheaper than late emergency response.

Worked example: cases appear in three villages with onsets clustering at 10 to 14 day intervals and all cases attended the same funeral. The pattern of successive generations and a common event suggests person-to-person spread seeded by a funeral exposure. Control: trace and monitor funeral attendees, offer safe burial teams, and vaccinate contacts and contacts of contacts if a vaccine exists.

lessons.title: WHO and the International Health Regulations
body: The World Health Organization is a specialised agency of the United Nations whose Constitution was adopted in 1946; it came into being in 1948. Its governing body is the World Health Assembly, in which every member state has one vote, and its executive is led by a Director-General elected by the Assembly on the nomination of the Executive Board. The Constitution defines health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease, and names the highest attainable standard of health as a fundamental right of every human being. Its work covers norm-setting (guidelines, the Essential Medicines List, classifications), technical support to countries, coordination of emergency response, and convening.

WHO is limited by design. It cannot compel states and has no police or enforcement arm. Most of its funding comes from voluntary contributions, largely earmarked by donors for specific programmes, rather than from assessed membership fees, which gives donors influence over priorities and makes budgets less predictable. As of this writing, funding stress and the announced withdrawal of at least one major member have prompted budget cuts and reform discussions.

The International Health Regulations (2005), in force since 2007 and legally binding on states parties, are the main legal instrument for managing cross-border health threats. They require countries to develop core capacities for surveillance and response, to assess events using a decision instrument and notify WHO within 24 hours of an assessment that an event may constitute a public health emergency of international concern, and to share information. The Director-General, after consulting an Emergency Committee, can determine that an event is a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) and issue temporary recommendations. Examples include the 2009 influenza H1N1 pandemic, polio (from 2014), Ebola in West Africa in 2014 and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2019, Zika in 2016, COVID-19 in 2020 and mpox in 2022 and again in 2024.

The IHR also cautions against unjustified travel and trade restrictions: measures that significantly interfere with international traffic should be based on scientific evidence and be no more restrictive than needed, and countries that exceed WHO advice must report their rationale. In practice many states have imposed restrictions anyway, and compliance, transparency and capacity gaps have been persistent criticisms. After COVID-19, states negotiated amendments to the IHR, adopted by the Assembly in 2024, which among other changes create a higher alert level called a pandemic emergency; as of this writing, the amendments are in force for most states, with some having rejected them. In 2025 the Assembly also adopted a separate WHO Pandemic Agreement, concerning prevention, preparedness, equitable access and benefit-sharing, whose annex on pathogen access and benefit sharing was still under negotiation, so its practical effect depends on that annex and on ratifications.

An honest assessment recognises two views. Supporters say that a binding framework with a trusted technical convenor gives smaller states access to expertise and a shared rulebook. Sceptics say that WHO has too little leverage over powerful states, can be slow to declare emergencies, and risks politicisation. Both points appear in the record, and the reform debate is about whether to strengthen financing and verification rather than whether coordination is needed.

Worked example: a state detects an unusual cluster of severe respiratory illness. Under the IHR it must assess the event using the decision instrument, notify WHO within 24 hours if it meets the criteria, and respond. The Director-General may convene the Emergency Committee, and if a PHEIC is declared, temporary recommendations are issued; they advise but do not command.

lessons.title: Pandemic Preparedness
body: Pandemic preparedness is the set of capacities that let a country or the world detect a new threat early, contain it quickly and limit harm if it spreads. A useful teaching frame has four parts: detect, respond, protect and pay. Detection means surveillance that can spot unusual events, laboratories that can identify pathogens, and genomic sequencing and data sharing that reveal how the pathogen changes. Response means trained workers, plans for contact tracing and isolation, and infection prevention and control in health facilities. Protection means medical countermeasures such as vaccines, diagnostics, therapeutics and protective equipment, together with community measures. Financing is what keeps the first three alive between emergencies, which is the hard part because the benefits are invisible when preparedness works.

Evaluating preparedness is itself difficult. WHO has promoted Joint External Evaluations, voluntary peer reviews of national capacities, and the Global Health Security Index scored countries in 2019. Experience with COVID-19 showed that high scores did not reliably predict performance, because outcomes also depended on trust in government, political leadership, communication, social cohesion and the ability to adapt. This is a good example of why composite indicators should be used with care.

Several issues dominate the post-COVID debate. First is speed and equity of countermeasures. Messenger RNA vaccines were developed and authorised in under a year, a scientific success, but early supply went largely to high-income countries. The COVAX Facility, a pooled purchasing and donation mechanism, delivered many doses to lower-income countries but fell short of its early goals, reflecting export restrictions, bilateral purchase deals and limited manufacturing capacity in low-income regions. Responses include regional manufacturing, technology transfer such as the mRNA hub in South Africa, and the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, whose stated aim is a vaccine within 100 days of a threat.

Second is data and sample sharing. Researchers need prompt access to pathogen sequences, while countries that provide samples want a fair share of the benefits, such as access to resulting products; these competing interests are at the heart of the pathogen access and benefit-sharing negotiations under the WHO Pandemic Agreement. Tension exists with the Nagoya Protocol on access to genetic resources under the Convention on Biological Diversity, which governs some biological resources by bilateral terms.

Third is finance. The Pandemic Fund, hosted by the World Bank and launched in 2022, provides grants to strengthen surveillance, laboratory capacity and workforce in lower-income countries, and demand has far exceeded available funds. Fourth is the role of non-pharmaceutical measures such as masks, ventilation, testing and travel measures, whose effects and costs, including harms to education and mental health, are still being studied, and where evidence quality varies by measure.

Fifth is the One Health perspective: since most emerging infections of humans originate in animals, surveillance at the animal-human-environment interface, through wildlife, farming and market monitoring, is part of preparedness.

Worked example: a country scores high on a preparedness index but suffers heavy early COVID-19 mortality. Analysis finds weak public trust and inconsistent messaging, low testing in the first weeks, and overwhelmed hospitals. The lesson is that capacity on paper does not equal capacity in practice, and that trust and communication are core components.

lessons.title: Noncommunicable Disease in a Global Setting
body: Noncommunicable diseases are chronic conditions that are not passed from person to person. WHO focuses on four groups: cardiovascular diseases, cancers, chronic respiratory diseases and diabetes, with mental health and injuries often considered alongside. They account for roughly three quarters of global deaths, and about three quarters of those deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries, where people also die earlier. Premature mortality in this setting is usually defined as death between ages 30 and 70, and the Sustainable Development Goals set a target of reducing premature noncommunicable disease mortality by one third by 2030.

Four shared behavioural risk factors drive much of the burden: tobacco use, harmful alcohol use, unhealthy diet and physical inactivity. Metabolic intermediates (raised blood pressure, glucose, lipids and body weight) link behaviour to disease, and environmental risk, notably air pollution, adds substantially. Because the same upstream causes feed several diseases, common risk factor approaches are efficient. The commercial determinants of health, meaning the influence of tobacco, alcohol, ultra-processed food and other industries on health, are an increasing focus of scholarship and policy.

The WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, adopted in 2003 and in force from 2005, is the first treaty negotiated under the WHO Constitution and has been joined by most states. It commits parties to measures including tax and price increases, smoke-free public places, health warnings and plain packaging, advertising bans, and support for cessation. Tobacco taxation is the best-studied intervention: demand falls as price rises, particularly among the young and the poor, and revenue can fund health. WHO's lists of cost-effective measures, often called best buys, include reducing salt intake, controlling harmful alcohol use through tax and availability, and treating hypertension and diabetes in primary care with simple protocols.

Hypertension illustrates the care cascade. It is highly prevalent worldwide, but in many countries only a minority of those affected are aware, treated and controlled. Low-cost generic drug classes, such as thiazide-like diuretics, calcium-channel blockers and ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, are effective, so the problem is system delivery: detection, supply, adherence and follow-up. WHO's HEARTS technical package promotes standard protocols, team-based care and reliable medicine supply at primary care level. Diabetes has a similar profile, with insulin access and affordability a persistent problem in poorer settings, along with cost of test strips.

Cancer prevention in low-resource settings favours measures with high yield. Cervical cancer, caused by persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus types, is largely preventable. WHO's strategy to eliminate it as a public health problem sets targets by 2030 for 90 percent of girls vaccinated by age 15, 70 percent of women screened with a high-performance test by 35 and again by 45, and 90 percent of those with pre-cancer or cancer treated. Hepatitis B vaccination reduces liver cancer, and tobacco control reduces lung and many other cancers.

Concerns exist about health systems designed around acute infectious disease: chronic care needs continuity, drug supply, patient education and out-of-pocket costs that do not become catastrophic. Debate continues over how to weigh prevention investments against treatment for those already ill, and over regulation versus personal responsibility; both appear in the policy record, and the evidence base favours taxes and regulation for their population-level effect with attention to equity.

Worked example: a primary care programme screens adults for hypertension, finds many untreated, and gives a standard stepped protocol with a combined once-daily pill and regular drug supply. Over a year control rates rise. The change came from system design, not a new drug.

lessons.title: Models of Health Systems
body: A health system includes every organisation, person and action whose primary intent is to improve health. Textbooks describe a few ideal types by who pays and who provides, and then admit that nearly every real country is a hybrid. The value of the models is that they make trade-offs visible.

The Beveridge model, named after William Beveridge and embodied in the British National Health Service launched in 1948, finances care from general taxation and often provides it through publicly owned hospitals and employed clinicians. Care is free or nearly free at the point of use, and the government sets budgets and can control costs through global budgets and gatekeeping by general practitioners. Strengths are universality and cost control; weaknesses can include waiting lists when budgets are tight and exposure to political budget cycles. Spain, Nordic countries and New Zealand follow versions of it.

The Bismarck model, associated with the sickness insurance law introduced in Germany in the 1880s, finances care through compulsory contributions from employers and employees to multiple non-profit sickness funds, with providers often private. Insurers are heavily regulated, must accept all applicants, and cover a standard benefit package; fees are negotiated collectively. Germany, France in a variant, Belgium and Japan are examples. Strengths include choice and responsiveness; weaknesses include administrative complexity and the need for subsidy to cover people outside formal work.

The national health insurance model, or single-payer model, mixes the two: providers are largely private, but a single government-run insurer collects premiums or taxes and pays all claims. Canada's provincial plans, Taiwan's system and South Korea's are standard examples. A single payer holds strong bargaining power over prices and has low administrative costs, though it may ration through waiting times and may limit what the public plan covers, leaving a role for supplemental private insurance. In the out-of-pocket model, common in poorer countries, only those who can pay obtain care, and the result is the opposite of coverage: catastrophic costs for those who need it.

Most countries mix elements. The United States combines employer-sponsored private insurance, public programmes for older and low-income people, and a large uninsured group, and is described as a patchwork rather than a single model. The Netherlands and Switzerland use regulated competing private insurers with mandates and subsidies. Mixed systems add private supplementary or complementary insurance on top of public coverage, as in many Beveridge countries.

When comparing, analysts use outcomes (life expectancy, avoidable mortality), access, financial protection, quality, spending per person and satisfaction. A common error is to attribute differences in outcomes to the health system alone; income, behaviour and social conditions contribute, so results must be read with caution. Another is to treat the labels as strict, because a country's model changes over time.

Worked example: a country finances care by payroll contributions to competing non-profit funds, has private clinics and hospitals, and mandates that insurers accept all applicants. This is a Bismarck-type system. If the same country replaced the funds with one public insurer paying private providers, it would have moved to a single-payer national health insurance model.

lessons.title: Health Financing and Universal Health Coverage
body: Universal health coverage means that all people can obtain the health services they need, of sufficient quality to be effective, without suffering financial hardship. Target 3.8 of the Sustainable Development Goals adopts this aim. It has two measured dimensions: service coverage (an index of essential services across reproductive, maternal and child health, infectious disease, noncommunicable disease and service capacity) and financial protection.

Financing is analysed through three functions. Revenue raising collects funds from general taxes, social health insurance contributions, voluntary private insurance, out-of-pocket payments and external aid. Pooling combines funds so that financial risk is shared across healthy and sick people; larger, more diverse pools spread risk better, and fragmentation into many small schemes weakens it. Purchasing is how pooled funds are spent on services. Methods include fee-for-service, which pays per item and encourages volume; capitation, a fixed payment per enrolled person that encourages efficiency but risks under-provision; diagnosis-related groups, paying a fixed amount per case type; and global budgets for institutions. No payment method is neutral; each creates incentives that must be monitored.

Out-of-pocket payment is the worst form of financing for equity because it ties access to ability to pay at the moment of need. Two measures of its harm are common. Catastrophic health expenditure is spending above a threshold share of household resources, often 10 percent or 25 percent of total consumption or income. Impoverishment is when health spending pushes a household below the poverty line. The share of households facing these outcomes is the Sustainable Development Goals' financial protection indicator. User fees were promoted in the 1980s to raise revenue but lowered use among the poor; several countries, including Uganda in 2001, later abolished them in public facilities, with a large rise in attendance but also with pressure on supplies and staff.

Countries have extended coverage in different ways. Thailand's Universal Coverage Scheme, launched in 2002, covers people outside formal employment using tax funding and capitation-based payments to providers, with a small copayment initially. Rwanda built community-based health insurance schemes with subsidies. Brazil's constitution of 1988 made health a right and created a unified health system. Mexico's Seguro Popular was later restructured. These show that universal coverage has been achieved at various income levels, though sustainability depends on political commitment and fiscal space.

The Abuja Declaration of 2001 committed African Union members to allocate at least 15 percent of their national budgets to health, a target most have not met. Evidence also shows that prepayment and pooling matter more than the label on the system. Debate remains about how large a benefit package can be, how to prioritise using cost-effectiveness and equity, and how to cover informal workers, who are a large share of workforces in many countries. Moral hazard, the tendency of insured people to use more care, is a concern for insurers, but evidence suggests that the harm of uncovered need, which is not just unnecessary demand, is larger in low-income settings.

Worked example: a family in a country without insurance sells land to pay for a caesarean section that costs 40 percent of annual household income. This counts as catastrophic spending under both common thresholds and may push the household into poverty. A pooled tax-funded scheme with no fee at the point of use would prevent it.

lessons.title: Essential Medicines and Access
body: Essential medicines are those that satisfy the priority health care needs of a population, selected with regard to disease burden, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness. WHO published its first Model List of Essential Medicines in 1977 and updates it roughly every two years through an expert committee. National lists adapted from it guide procurement and reimbursement. The concept is a rational use tool: a short list of well-chosen drugs is easier to procure, store, prescribe and monitor than a long list of near duplicates.

Access has several barriers that must be separated. Availability is whether the medicine is in stock; affordability is whether people or the system can pay; quality means the product contains the right drug in the right dose; and rational use means it is prescribed and taken appropriately. Poor-quality medicines fall into substandard products, which fail specifications through error or poor manufacture, and falsified products, which deliberately misrepresent identity or source. Regulatory capacity and prequalification schemes, such as WHO prequalification used by procurers, help to assure quality. Many low-income countries also face stock-outs from poor forecasting and supply chain weaknesses, not only from high prices.

Intellectual property rules shape price. The WTO's Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS), in force from 1995, requires member states to provide 20 years of patent protection, including for pharmaceuticals. Supporters argue that patents reward costly research and development. Critics argue that monopoly pricing denies life-saving drugs to poor people. TRIPS includes flexibilities: governments may grant compulsory licences allowing generic production without the patent holder's consent, subject to conditions, and may allow parallel importation. The Doha Declaration of 2001 affirmed that TRIPS should be interpreted in support of public health and each member's right to protect it.

The AIDS crisis was a turning point. In the late 1990s antiretroviral therapy cost in the order of ten thousand dollars per person per year, out of reach in Africa. South Africa's Medicines Act of 1997 and the legal challenge by pharmaceutical companies, which they dropped in 2001 under public pressure, became a symbol. In 2001 the Indian generic manufacturer Cipla offered triple therapy at a fraction of the prevailing price, and competition drove prices down by well over 90 percent in following years. A further problem was that countries lacking manufacturing capacity could not benefit from compulsory licences; a 2003 decision of the WTO General Council, later made a permanent amendment to TRIPS, allowed export of generics made under compulsory licence to such countries, though it has been used rarely because of procedural complexity.

Other mechanisms address gaps. The Medicines Patent Pool, set up in 2010 with UNITAID support, negotiates voluntary licences from patent holders for HIV, hepatitis C and other medicines. Pooled procurement through Gavi, the Global Fund and the Global Drug Facility lowers prices by aggregating demand. Product development partnerships such as the Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative develop treatments for diseases that offer little market return. Tiered pricing can help but is limited by leakage and by middle-income countries not always qualifying.

Worked example: a middle-income country faces a patented hepatitis C drug at a price that would consume its treatment budget. Options include negotiating a voluntary licence through a patent pool, invoking a compulsory licence under TRIPS flexibilities, or tendering for generic versions where patents do not apply. Each carries trade-offs of diplomacy, time and quality assurance.

lessons.title: Primary Health Care and the Health Workforce
body: Primary health care is both a level of care and a philosophy. The Declaration of Alma-Ata, adopted at a WHO and UNICEF conference in 1978 in what was then the Soviet Union, defined primary health care as essential care made universally accessible, based on practical, scientifically sound and socially acceptable methods, at a cost the community and country can afford. It called for Health for All by the year 2000, emphasised community participation and action across sectors, and framed health as a human right. The target date was missed, but the framework endured.

There was an early debate about scope. Selective primary health care, proposed in 1979 by Julia Walsh and Kenneth Warren, argued that limited resources should go first to a few cost-effective interventions against the leading causes of child death, such as immunisation, oral rehydration, breastfeeding promotion and growth monitoring. Supporters of the comprehensive model argued that this approach neglected social determinants and community ownership. Both strands influenced later practice, and the choice is better seen as a question of sequencing and emphasis than a pure either-or. The 2018 Declaration of Astana renewed the commitment to primary health care as the route to universal coverage, with emphasis on integrated services, empowered people and communities, and supportive policy.

Evidence shows that health systems oriented to primary care tend to produce better population health and lower costs, mainly through continuity, prevention and appropriate referral. Examples include Brazil's Family Health Strategy, where teams including community agents are assigned to defined populations, and Ethiopia's Health Extension Programme, which trained and deployed female health extension workers to villages from 2003 to deliver a package of preventive and basic curative services. Evaluations suggest gains in service use, although quality and supervision remain challenges.

The workforce is the binding constraint in many places. WHO projects a shortfall of roughly ten million health workers by 2030, concentrated in low-income countries, particularly in Africa and parts of Asia. Reasons include limited training capacity, low pay, poor working conditions, maldistribution toward cities, and international migration, sometimes called brain drain, in which health workers move from poorer to richer countries. The WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel, adopted in 2010, is a voluntary code that encourages ethical recruitment and calls on destination countries to avoid actively recruiting from countries with critical shortages. Because it is voluntary, enforcement is weak.

Responses to shortage include task shifting, in which tasks are moved to less specialised cadres such as clinical officers, nurses and community health workers, provided with training, supervision and referral; this approach is supported by trials in HIV treatment and maternal and child health. Community health workers can raise coverage of services, but programmes that underpay them, give no supplies or supervision, or rely on unpaid labour from women are fragile; this has led to calls for formal recognition and fair pay.

Worked example: a country needs more skilled birth coverage. It could train more doctors, a slow and costly step, or train more midwives, who can safely deliver most births when supported by referral for complications. The task-shifting evidence favours expanding midwifery in the short term while building referral capacity.

lessons.title: Ethics of Global Health Research
body: Modern research ethics grew out of abuses. The Nuremberg Code of 1947, written in the judgment of the trial of Nazi physicians, put voluntary informed consent first. The World Medical Association's Declaration of Helsinki, first issued in 1964 and revised many times, is the principal professional statement for medical research and requires ethics committee review, risk-benefit assessment, and special protection for vulnerable groups. In the United States the Belmont Report of 1979, produced after the Tuskegee syphilis study came to light, named three principles: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. The Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences issued guidelines that apply these principles to research in low-resource settings, including community engagement and the obligations of sponsors.

International research raises distinctive problems. Consent may involve low literacy, community or household decision-makers, and unequal relationships between researchers and participants; good practice uses translated materials, oral processes with witnesses, comprehension checks and engagement with community leaders, but individual consent should not be replaced by community permission. Vulnerability can arise from poverty, weak health care access and limited alternatives, which leads to concerns about undue inducement when participants receive payments or health services that they could not otherwise obtain. Review requires both the sponsor's and host country's ethics committees, since local committees understand local context and may have limited resources to review complex trials.

The best-known controversy involves the placebo-controlled trials of short-course zidovudine to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission in the 1990s. After a 1994 trial showed that a long regimen reduced transmission, studies in developing countries tested cheaper shorter regimens against placebo. Critics, including Peter Lurie and Sidney Wolfe, argued that a placebo group was unethical when an effective regimen existed, because participants were denied a proven treatment. Defenders argued that the long regimen was not feasible or available in the host countries, that the local standard of care was no treatment, and that a placebo-controlled design gave faster, clearer answers useful to those populations. The dispute exposed the question of whether the control arm should be the best proven intervention worldwide or the local standard of care. Later revisions of the Declaration of Helsinki state that a new intervention should generally be tested against the best proven intervention, and permit placebo only when no proven intervention exists or when compelling and scientifically sound reasons exist and participants will not face added risk of serious harm.

Other concerns include post-trial access: whether participants and their communities should receive an effective product after the study. Helsinki says that sponsors, researchers and governments should plan for post-trial provisions. Related is the problem of exploitation, in which a trial uses low-income participants to produce a product that will be sold mainly in wealthy markets; the reasonable availability debate asks what benefits the community is owed. Critics also describe parachute or helicopter research, in which researchers from wealthy institutions collect data and samples and leave with the credit, and call for capacity-building, shared authorship, local leadership and fair governance of data and biological samples.

Another strand concerns open questions, where reasonable people disagree. Some hold that research on poor populations is justified when it addresses their health problems and treats them as partners; others emphasise vulnerability and insist on high protection. The more settled consensus is that responsiveness to local health needs, scientific validity, independent review and fair benefits are all required.

Worked example: a sponsor from a wealthy country proposes a vaccine trial in a low-income country with a placebo arm, although an effective vaccine exists but is unaffordable locally. The ethics committee should ask whether the placebo is justified, whether participants will face serious harm, whether the product would be available afterwards, and whether the local committee has had a full review.

lessons.title: Humanitarian Medicine in Conflict and Disaster
body: Humanitarian medicine delivers care to people affected by conflict, disaster, displacement and epidemics. It is guided by four humanitarian principles: humanity (alleviating suffering wherever found), impartiality (aid based on need alone, without discrimination), neutrality (not taking sides in hostilities or controversies) and independence (autonomy from political, military or economic objectives). They are not decorative; they are what lets aid workers negotiate access with armed parties. Debates exist about how far neutrality can be sustained when an organisation also speaks about abuses it witnesses.

The legal frame is international humanitarian law. The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their Additional Protocols of 1977 protect the wounded and sick, medical personnel, units and transport, which may not be attacked and must be respected, provided they are not used to commit acts harmful to the enemy. Attacks on hospitals are among the most serious violations, and monitoring systems record such attacks. The Convention relating to the Status of Refugees of 1951 defines a refugee and sets the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning a person to a place where they face persecution. Internally displaced people, who have not crossed a border, are not covered by that convention but are covered by general human rights and humanitarian law.

Organisations differ in style. The International Committee of the Red Cross and Red Crescent movement works under mandates in the Geneva Conventions and traditionally favours confidential dialogue with parties to a conflict. Médecins Sans Frontières, founded in 1971 by French doctors, emphasises témoignage, or bearing witness, and will speak publicly about abuses. These are two ways of weighing access against advocacy, and neither is obviously correct; each has costs.

In the acute phase of a crisis, public health priorities are well described. A crude mortality rate above one death per 10,000 people per day is a standard emergency threshold, and child mortality thresholds are higher. The leading killers are measles, diarrhoeal diseases, acute respiratory infection, malaria where endemic and malnutrition, driven by crowding, poor water and sanitation, and disrupted services. Priorities include safe water and sanitation, shelter, food, vaccination against measles, oral rehydration, outbreak surveillance and treatment of severe acute malnutrition. Ready-to-use therapeutic food allows many children with severe malnutrition and an appetite to be treated at home. The Sphere Handbook sets minimum standards for water, shelter, food and health response. The cluster approach, led for health by WHO, coordinates agencies.

Mass casualty events require triage, which sorts patients by urgency and survivability to do the greatest good with limited resources, often using colour categories such as immediate, delayed, minimal and expectant. This is an application of utilitarian reasoning, different from ordinary practice, and it is justified by scarcity. Other ethical issues include whether aid prolongs conflict by feeding armed groups, how to avoid creating parallel systems that undermine local health services, and obligations to local staff, who carry most of the risk.

Worked example: a camp of 30,000 displaced people reports a crude mortality rate of 2 per 10,000 per day, mostly from diarrhoea and measles in children. This exceeds the emergency threshold. Priorities are clean water and latrines, measles vaccination, oral rehydration and treatment of malnourished children, together with surveillance for further outbreaks.

lessons.title: Antimicrobial Resistance and One Health
body: Antimicrobial resistance occurs when microbes evolve so that drugs that once killed them no longer work. The mechanism is natural selection: in a population of bacteria, a few carry resistance traits through mutation or through acquired genes; when an antibiotic is used, susceptible bacteria die and resistant ones survive and multiply. Resistance genes can also move between bacteria by horizontal gene transfer on plasmids, which allows resistance to spread across species. Every use of an antibiotic exerts selection pressure, so inappropriate use accelerates the problem, although even appropriate use contributes some.

Mechanisms of resistance include enzymes that destroy the drug (beta-lactamases that break the beta-lactam ring), changes in the drug target (the altered penicillin-binding protein of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), efflux pumps that expel the drug, and reduced permeability. Important resistant groups include MRSA, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producing Enterobacterales, and carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales and Acinetobacter, for which few treatment options remain. The discovery in 2015 of the mcr-1 gene, conferring plasmid-borne resistance to colistin, a last-line antibiotic, in animals and humans in China, illustrated how resistance in one sector can reach another.

The One Health approach recognises that human, animal and environmental health are linked. Drivers include overprescribing in human medicine, antibiotics sold without prescription, incomplete courses, poor infection control in hospitals, inadequate sanitation that spreads resistant organisms, use of antibiotics in livestock for growth promotion or routine prevention, and pharmaceutical pollution in waterways. A widely cited modelling study in the Global Research on Antimicrobial Resistance project estimated about 1.27 million deaths in 2019 directly attributable to bacterial resistance and about 4.95 million deaths associated with it (approximate), with the highest burden in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. The 2024 United Nations General Assembly political declaration set targets that include reducing deaths associated with antimicrobial resistance by 10 percent by 2030 against the 2019 baseline.

Responses are layered. Infection prevention and control, hand hygiene, clean water and vaccination reduce the need for antibiotics; vaccines against pneumococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b, for example, reduce both infections and prescriptions. Antimicrobial stewardship programmes promote right drug, dose, duration and route and use diagnostics to separate bacterial from viral infection. WHO's AWaRe classification groups antibiotics into Access (first- or second-choice antibiotics with a lower resistance potential), Watch (higher resistance potential, to be used for specific indications) and Reserve (last-resort drugs). Surveillance systems track resistance, and many countries restrict growth-promoter use in animals.

There is also an economic problem: new antibiotics are used sparingly to preserve effectiveness and are given for short courses, so sales are low and companies lack incentive to develop them. Proposed solutions include pull incentives, such as subscription-style payments that delink revenue from volume, and public funding of early research. Another tension is access: many deaths from bacterial infection occur because people cannot reach any effective antibiotic, so stewardship should not restrict use where access is poor. Both excess and access problems coexist, and policy must address both.

Worked example: a hospital sees a rise in carbapenem-resistant infections. Response includes screening and isolating colonised patients, reinforcing hand hygiene and environmental cleaning, reviewing carbapenem prescribing, and reporting to the national surveillance system. Giving more carbapenems would worsen the selection pressure.

lessons.title: The Right to Health, Aid and Equity in Global Governance
body: The right to health is set out in Article 12 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights of 1966, which recognises the right of everyone to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health. The Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, in General Comment 14 of 2000, interpreted it as a right to timely and appropriate health care and also to underlying determinants such as safe water, sanitation, food, housing and healthy working conditions. It identified four essential features: availability, accessibility (including non-discrimination, physical and economic access, and information access), acceptability (culturally appropriate and respectful of medical ethics) and quality. The Covenant provides for progressive realisation, meaning states must take steps to the maximum of available resources, but some core obligations, such as non-discrimination and essential medicines, are immediate. Critics question how enforceable such rights are; defenders point to national courts that have ordered treatment access, for example in HIV medicine cases.

Global health is financed through a mix. Development assistance for health flows from bilateral donors, multilateral agencies and philanthropic foundations, and sizeable programmes such as the Global Fund, Gavi and the United States President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief have been associated with major declines in AIDS and child deaths. Domestic public spending is the larger source in most countries as incomes grow, and the transition from aid dependence to self-financing is a recurring policy theme, along with questions on debt, fiscal space and who sets priorities. Aid is also volatile; abrupt reductions in funding by major donors, as occurred around 2025 in several programmes, can disrupt treatment supply and surveillance, so contingency planning is needed.

A long-running debate concerns vertical versus horizontal approaches. Vertical programmes target single diseases with dedicated funds, supply lines and targets, and can deliver measurable results quickly. Critics argue they fragment systems, draw skilled staff away from general services and reflect donor rather than national priorities. Defenders point to evidence that disease programmes have built laboratory, supply and data capacity, and that in some places they were the only route to scale. Many analysts now advocate integration and health system strengthening, with disease programmes designed to support the system rather than bypass it. The Paris Declaration on Aid Effectiveness of 2005 set principles of national ownership, alignment with country systems and harmonisation among donors.

Questions of power have become prominent. Scholars and practitioners describe the legacy of colonial medicine, the dominance of institutions in wealthy countries in agenda-setting, authorship and funding, and unequal partnerships in which local staff do the work while foreign partners hold the grants. The movement to decolonise global health calls for local leadership, shared decision-making, equitable authorship, direct funding of local institutions and, for some, a rethinking of the field's assumptions. Others caution that the term is used loosely and that the practical measures, funding flows and governance, should be specified and tested.

Climate change adds a further dimension: heat, floods, changing vector ranges, food insecurity and displacement fall hardest on populations that have contributed least to emissions, which links health equity to climate policy.

Worked example: a donor funds an HIV programme with its own parallel supply chain and data system. Ten years later the donor reduces funding. Where the programme was integrated into the national system, treatment continues with domestic financing; where it was a separate structure, services collapse. The case illustrates why alignment with country systems matters.

questions.prompt: The DALY is calculated as the sum of which two components?
choices: Years of life lost to premature death plus years of healthy life expectancy
Years lived with disability plus years of treatment received by patients
Years of potential income lost plus years lived with disability
Years of life lost to premature death plus years lived with disability

questions.prompt: A health ministry compares two programmes using cost per DALY averted. Why is this metric useful for priority-setting?
choices: It measures only the number of lives saved, regardless of the age at death
It removes the need to estimate uncertainty because it relies on exact registry data
It combines deaths prevented and disability avoided into a single comparable unit across diseases
It guarantees the cheapest programme is also the one preferred by affected communities

questions.prompt: Which condition is most likely to rank higher by DALYs than by number of deaths?
choices: Neonatal sepsis in a hospital
Major depressive disorder
Acute myocardial infarction
Rabies after a dog bite

questions.prompt: Country A has 500 deaths from a disease, each at an age with 30 years of remaining life expectancy. Country B has 4,000 people with a chronic condition of disability weight 0.25 lasting 5 years each. Which statement best compares total burden?
choices: Country A has 15,000 DALYs and Country B has 5,000, so A has the larger burden
Country A has 15,000 DALYs and Country B has 20,000, so B has the larger burden
Country A has 500 DALYs and Country B has 4,000, so B has the larger burden
Country A has 15,000 DALYs and Country B has 1,000, so A has the larger burden

questions.prompt: Between two years a low-income country reports a large rise in recorded noncommunicable-disease deaths, while infection deaths are unchanged. Which interpretation is most defensible before concluding the disease pattern has changed?
choices: The disability weights must have been revised upward in that single country, which would raise the recorded number of noncommunicable-disease deaths in a single year
The country has completed the epidemiologic transition and no longer has a double burden, which is shown by a rise in recorded noncommunicable deaths
Infection deaths must be falling because deaths cannot rise in one category without falling in another, so the unchanged figure must be an error
Improved death registration and cause-of-death certification may be revealing deaths previously unrecorded or miscoded

questions.prompt: Which finding from the Whitehall studies best illustrates the social gradient in health?
choices: Mortality rose stepwise as civil service grade fell, even among people with stable jobs
Only the lowest-paid grade showed higher mortality, with no difference among the others
Mortality was the same across grades once smoking was recorded in the survey
Higher-grade civil servants had worse health because of greater work responsibility

questions.prompt: A city taxes sugar-sweetened drinks and subsidises school meals. In the downstream-upstream framework, these are best described as which kind of action?
choices: Midstream only, because they affect individual behaviour without any policy
Upstream, because they change the conditions that shape exposure across a population
Downstream, because they treat the illness after it develops in individuals
Downstream, because they depend on individual clinicians prescribing a change

questions.prompt: Which of the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health (2008) overarching recommendations is correctly stated?
choices: Prioritise hospital construction over community-level action everywhere
Limit health policy to the health ministry to avoid conflict with other sectors
Tackle the inequitable distribution of power, money and resources
Replace national health systems with a single global service provider

questions.prompt: A study finds that people in poor health later earn less. A researcher claims low income therefore causes ill health. What is the most important weakness in that inference?
choices: Selection of too many participants, which makes confidence intervals unreliable
Lack of a control for the number of clinics in the area, which is the true cause
The use of income rather than education, since only education affects health
Reverse causation: ill health may have caused the fall in income rather than the reverse

questions.prompt: Two districts have equal clinic numbers but life expectancy differs by twelve years. Which proposed response is best aligned with the social determinants evidence?
choices: Assess housing, air quality, employment and food access and act on the largest modifiable gaps alongside clinical services
Double the clinic staffing in the poorer district and expect the gap to close entirely, since the number of clinical contacts is the main determinant of life expectancy
Attribute the gap to individual lifestyle choices and fund a media campaign only, since social conditions have little influence on health once clinics are equally available
Conclude that no action is possible because the gap reflects fixed genetic differences between the populations, which public policy cannot change in a short period

questions.prompt: In the demographic transition, which change typically comes first?
choices: Migration replaces births as the main driver of growth
Death rates fall, producing rapid population growth
Birth rates fall, producing rapid population ageing
Birth rates rise as living standards improve

questions.prompt: A household contains a stunted child and an overweight mother. This is a typical example of which concept?
choices: The double burden of malnutrition
Concentration of health care in the richest quintile
Reverse causation between income and disease
A completed epidemiologic transition

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes equality from equity in health?
choices: Equality means resources are allocated according to need, and equity means identical shares
Equity applies only between countries, and equality only within a single country
Equity is a statistical measure and equality is purely an ethical principle
Equity may require unequal resources so that avoidable, unfair differences in health are reduced
