questions.prompt: Under-five mortality in the poorest quintile falls from 120 to 90 per 1,000, and in the richest from 40 to 10. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: The absolute gap widened to 110 while the ratio fell from 3 to 2
Both the absolute gap and the ratio were unchanged because both groups improved

Admitting more refugees than a state has housing for, so that states cannot be required to receive more people than they can accommodate
Giving food aid to people who have not registered, so that assistance may be given only to those whose status has been verified by the host state
Treating wounded combatants of the opposing side, so that medical staff may care only for casualties of the party that has authority over the area

questions.prompt: A crude mortality rate above what level is conventionally used as an emergency threshold in humanitarian settings?
choices: One death per 1,000 people per year
Ten deaths per 100,000 people per month
Five deaths per 1,000 people per week
One death per 10,000 people per day

questions.prompt: A displaced camp reports a crude mortality rate of 2 per 10,000 per day, with most deaths from diarrhoea, measles and malnutrition in children. Which set of priorities is best?
choices: Building a tertiary referral hospital before any other service, since specialist surgery is the intervention that most reduces deaths from diarrhoea and measles in camps
Registration of all residents and issuing of identity documents before any medical intervention, because services cannot be provided until population numbers are verified
Safe water and sanitation, measles vaccination, oral rehydration and malnutrition treatment, with outbreak surveillance
Long-term cancer screening, chronic disease clinics and elective surgery, because these have the largest effect on mortality in the acute phase of a displacement emergency

questions.prompt: One agency keeps its observations of abuses confidential to preserve access to detainees. Another publicly denounces abuses even if it risks expulsion. How should this difference be understood?
choices: Public denunciation is required of all agencies under the Geneva Conventions
Two defensible strategies weighing access against advocacy, each with costs
One approach violates humanitarian law and the other complies with it
Only confidential approaches are compatible with neutrality

questions.prompt: Which process best explains how antibiotic resistance becomes common in a bacterial population?
choices: Selection: the drug kills susceptible bacteria and resistant ones survive and multiply
Adaptation: bacteria deliberately change in response to a drug they detect
Immunity: patients who take antibiotics become resistant themselves
Mutation only: resistance appears in every cell after drug exposure

questions.prompt: In WHO's AWaRe classification, what does the Reserve group contain?
choices: Antiviral drugs reserved for epidemic use
Last-resort antibiotics to be saved for infections caused by multidrug-resistant organisms
First-choice antibiotics with low resistance potential used for common infections
Antibiotics with higher resistance potential used only for specific indications

questions.prompt: Why is the discovery of the plasmid-borne mcr-1 gene considered significant?
choices: It allows bacteria to survive without a cell wall in all environments, and it has been found only in laboratory strains that have no relevance to clinical infection
It is found only in laboratory strains and has no clinical relevance, because plasmids cannot move between bacteria outside of a controlled experimental environment
It confers transferable resistance to colistin, a last-line antibiotic, and spreads between bacteria and across species
It makes bacteria immune to all vaccines, and it has been found in every hospital pathogen, which makes infection control and immunisation ineffective in all settings

questions.prompt: A hospital sees a rise in carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales infections. Which response is most likely to reduce spread?
choices: Increasing empirical carbapenem use for all febrile patients to cover resistant organisms, because broader coverage reduces the number of patients who go untreated on admission
Stopping surveillance to avoid alarming staff and patients, because reporting of resistant organisms reduces confidence in the hospital without changing transmission
Relying on a single new antibiotic without changes to infection control, because a new drug makes screening and isolation unnecessary for colonised patients
Screening and isolating colonised patients, reinforcing hand hygiene and cleaning, and reviewing carbapenem prescribing

questions.prompt: A minister proposes banning antibiotic sales without prescription in a rural region where no clinic is within a day's travel. What is the most balanced analysis?
choices: The measure may reduce misuse but could block access to life-saving treatment, so it should be paired with improved access to prescribers and diagnostics
The measure is certain to eliminate resistance within a year, since non-prescription sales are the only driver of resistance, and access to clinics is therefore irrelevant to the policy decision
The measure is mistaken because resistance comes only from agriculture, so restrictions on human sales have no effect and the minister should regulate livestock use alone
Access is irrelevant to resistance policy, so the ban should be enforced at once and any resulting untreated infections should be accepted as the price of stewardship

questions.prompt: Which treaty article sets out the right to the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health?
choices: Article 12 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
Article 2 of the Geneva Convention on Refugees
Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
Article 7 of the Declaration of Alma-Ata

questions.prompt: According to General Comment 14, which set lists the essential features of the right to health?
choices: Sovereignty, solidarity, subsidiarity and sustainability
Availability, accessibility, acceptability and quality
Affordability, efficiency, equity and ethics
Prevention, treatment, rehabilitation and palliation

questions.prompt: What is the main criticism of vertical disease programmes?
choices: They prevent any domestic financing of health, because donors forbid governments from spending their own money on the targeted disease or on any related service
They are legally prohibited by the Paris Declaration, which bans earmarked funding and requires donors to give all assistance as general budget support
They can fragment health systems and draw staff away from general services while reflecting donor priorities
They never produce measurable results, so donors have abandoned them, and national governments now fund every disease entirely from domestic revenue without any external programmes

questions.prompt: A donor ends funding for an HIV programme run with its own parallel supply chain. In a neighbouring country, a similar programme was integrated into national systems. What outcome does the integration argument predict?
choices: Both programmes collapse equally because HIV services need donor funds, and the way a programme is organised has no effect on whether services survive a funding reduction
The parallel programme survives because donors build stronger systems than governments, so the separate supply chain is likelier to continue after external funding ends
Neither is affected because treatment does not require supply chains, so a reduction in donor funding has no effect on the availability of medicines or testing
The integrated programme is likelier to continue with domestic financing, while the parallel structure is likelier to collapse

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the debate about decolonising global health?
choices: Advocates call for local leadership, equitable authorship and direct funding, while some caution that the practical measures need to be specified and tested
All commentators agree that colonial history has no relevance to current global health, and the movement concerns only the choice of language used in conference presentations and publications
The movement argues that all global health funding should be stopped, while critics argue that funding should continue unchanged with no change in governance or authorship practices
The movement argues that only institutions in wealthy countries should hold grants, while critics argue that local institutions should receive funds directly without any partnership
